location: Chapel Bar Beach, Padstow, Cornwall, PL28 8DB
notes: Chapel Bar Beach lies at the mouth of the River Camel in North Cornwall, just a 10-minute walk from the charming fishing port of Padstow between Chidley Pumps (Lower beach) and St George's Well Cove. At low tide, a vast, wide expanse of sand is revealed which stretches for around 1½ miles along the Camel Estuary. Take in spectacular views of the Camel estuary from the beach and Daymer Bay on the opposite side. At high tide most of the beach is submerged along with the 'Doom Bar' sand bank, which protects the estuary from the strength of the Atlantic. Folklore tells of the ‘Doom Bar’ being created by the curse of a dying mermaid in revenge, and has been responsible for more than 600 shipwrecks since records began.

Dogs are banned on the beach at Sennen Cove from the 15th May – 30th September from 10am – 6pm (2023). Lifeguard cover is from Easter until the end of October (2023). Sennen Cove Beach was the winner of a Seaside Award in 2024. The South West Coast Path offers access north to Gwinver Beach. The Pedn-men-du, a promontory at the southern end of the bay, protects the cove from the westerly Atlantic gales. The beach is more popular as a surfing destination, but there can be excellent swimming on days with gentler winds and a smaller swell. Ensure you always swim between the red and yellow flags. There is a seasonal dog ban in place on the beach at Sennen Cove from the 15th of May to the 30th of September, between 10am and 6pm. Dogs are welcome at all other times.

Porthmeor Beach, St Ives, Cornwall, TR26 2BN. Seasonal dog ban from 15th of May to 30th September, between 10am and 6pm. Lifeguards patrolling from Easter to the start of November, between 10am and 6pm. Soft, sandy beach between two headlands. South West Coast Path passes through Porthmeor. Tate St Ives gallery located just behind the beach. Surfing is the main activity, with consistent and high quality waves. Rock pools available at the west end of the beach. Local stand up paddleboarding and bodyboard hire available. Large car park at St Ives Rugby Football Club, about a 20 minute walk from Porthmeor. Buses travel to the beach, including the 16 bus, 200 bus, and Land's End Coaster.

location: Crackington Haven, Bude, Cornwall, EX23 9JG
notes: Crackington Haven is an unspoiled sand and shingle cove nestled between imposing cliffs. The beach is ideal for families and surfers, with the tide revealing rock pools and sheltering sea life. A bistro café and family pub are nearby, along with toilet facilities and a small outlet for beach items. The area is popular with geologists and tourists due to its spectacular sedimentary rock formations, including the Crackington Formation. Lifeguards are on patrol between 10am-6pm each day throughout the summer holiday. There is a seasonal dog ban on the beach between the 15th of May and the 30th of September, from 10am to 6pm. Dogs are welcome at all other times. Parking is available at a pay and display car park in the centre of the village, with some roadside parking spots on Mill Ball Hill.

Dogs are currently allowed on Perranporth Beach all year around. Swimmers can take a dip in the clear waters of the surf, or if the waves aren't to your liking, relax in the Chapel Rock tidal pool. Surfers can expect to ride a fantastic break in one of Cornwall's prime surfing locations, with an incredible view of the coast to keep them company on their board. Be sure to take advantage of the numerous surf schools scattered about the beach and town, offering lesson levels ranging from newcomer to advanced. The beach is RNLI lifeguarded through early April to the end of October.

location: Cadgwith Cove Beach, Cadgwith, Cornwall, TR12 7JZ
notes: Dogs are banned from the beach in July and August between the hours of 10am and 6pm.

Mother Ivey's Bay is located in Trevose Head, Padstow, Cornwall, PL28 8SL. It is nestled on the North Coast between Trevose Head and Stepper Point. The bay is part of the Carnewas to Stepper Point Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty. The beach is suitable for swimmers, paddle boarders, and surfers on windy days. The surrounding area includes coastal paths. The RNLI Padstow Lifeboat Station is at the north end of the bay and is open to visitors 10am to 4pm on weekdays. Dogs are welcome all year round but must be kept on a lead between 10am and 6pm. There is no parking at Mother Ivey's Bay; visitors must use the National Trust Car Park at Trevose Head or Harlyn Bay Car Park.

location: Castle Beach, Falmouth, Cornwall, TR11 4NZ
notes: Dogs are welcome on this beach except between July 1st and August 31st when a seasonal dog ban is in place between 10am and 6pm.

location: Whitsand Bay
notes: The beaches of Whitsand Bay offer over three miles of stunning golden sand stretching from Rame Head west to Portwrinkle, and are considered one of Cornwall’s hidden gems. Reached by steep paths and steps that wind down between the verdant vegetation, Whitsand Bay beaches are never crowded. At low tide the long stretch of glistening sand provides great walking, whilst the consistent swell keeps surfers coming year-round. Rock pools dotted along the beach reveal fascinating marine life, and out to sea the bay is a popular dive site, home to HMS Scylla, an ex-naval frigate sunk in 2004 to form an artificial reef.

Porthtowan Beach is an RNLI lifeguarded beach, patrolled from around the beginning of May to the last weekend of September between 10am and 6pm. The beach is additionally patrolled in the Easter school holidays and October half-term, as well as some weekends outside of this time period. Please check the RNLI website for specific dates. There is a seasonal dog ban in place at Porthtowan Beach from the 15th of May to the 30th of September, between 10am and 6pm. Dogs are welcome at all other times. West-facing Porthtowan Beach is well regarded for its Atlantic swell, with perfect curling waves when the conditions are right. On these days the surf might be a bit too much to handle for a beginner, but when the wind isn't so strong Porthtowan is a fantastic place to learn to surf. Porthtowan has been a holder of the coveted Blue Flag award since 2005, which recognises the quality of its beach, environment, and amenities.

Accommodation: Holywell Bay, Nr Newquay, Cornwall, TR8 5PP. Car parking: Holywell Bay Car Park is a National Trust pay and display located on the west side of Holywell village, near the beach. The car park is free for National Trust members, or otherwise can be paid for by coins or with the PayByPhone app. Travelling by Bus: Several buses have lines travelling through Holywell Bay, including: the 850 between Newquay and Truro College; the 85 between Newquay and Truro; and the U1A Coast to Coast, between Falmouth and Newquay. Lifeguards: Holywell Bay Beach is patrolled by RNLI Lifeguards from mid-May to the last weekend of September. Dog friendly: Holywell Beach is dog friendly all year round. Film appearances: In Die Another Day (2002), starring Pierce Brosnan as James Bond, Holywell Bay was used to depict Bond's surfboard landing in North Korea. More recently, Holywell Bay portrayed Driftmark in the fantasy drama 'House of the Dragon' and has also been used in Poldark.

location: Gyllyngvase Beach, Cliff Road, Falmouth, Cornwall, TR11 4NA
notes: There is a seasonal restriction on dogs on the beach - restrictions are in place between 10am and 6pm from 15th May to 30th September. They are welcome on the beach at all other times.

location: Godrevy Beach, Gwithian, Hayle, Cornwall, TR27 5ED
notes: Godrevy Beach is a sandy cove that joins with Gwithian Beach at low tide to create one immense, golden crescent. Boasting prime positioning within St Ives Bay, the beach has spectacular views right out to St Ives one way and to Godrevy Lighthouse the other. There's plenty to do for everyone at Godrevy. On hot days, laze about on the beach while the sun bathes you from overhead and the kids play in the sand, or take a relaxing dip in the ocean. When the tide's out, go out and explore the rock pools in search of marine stragglers waiting for the next wave out. At the same time keep an eye out for the seals who love to keep an eye on you from a safe distance! Take a stroll along the cliffs beyond Godrevy, part of the Godrevy to Portreath Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty. On the headland you can gaze out at Godrevy Island, the inspiration for Virginia Woolf’s novel 'To The Lighthouse'. Follow the South West Coast Path east, looking down into Mutton Cove where the seals mass, and eventually you'll find yourself at Hell's Mouth, where dramatic cliffs drop down 300 feet into the sea. RNLI Lifeguards Hayle

location: Carne Beach, The Roseland, Cornwall, TR2 5AG
notes: Carne Beach is a National Trust owned beach situated on the beautiful Roseland Peninsula, facing south and overlooked by Nare Head rising 300 feet over the eastern side of Gerrans Bay. At high tide there is only a little beach until the waters retreat to reveal a generous shoreline of golden sands and shingle. Popular but never too busy, it’s a favourite for families, dog walks year-round and sometimes surfers, if the conditions are right. Access to the beach is down very narrow lanes. Dog friendly all year round, but please keep dogs under close control. Car park free to National Trust members, No overnight camping.

Seasonal dog ban in place at Porthcurno from the 1st of July and the 31st of August, between 10am and 6pm. Porthcurno Beach is patrolled by RNLI Lifeguards from mid-May to the last weekend of September. Access to Porthcurno is via a sandy path and steep steps. The beach is not wheelchair friendly. The Minack Theatre is a ten minute walk from Porthcurno Beach via the South West Coast Path.

Portreath Beach is a popular sandy cove loved by watersports enthusiasts and swimmers alike. Over on the north side of the beach is a tidal pool sheltered by the harbour wall, where swimmers who want to stay out of the swell can bask in peace. The beach itself produces a half decent wave, but it's "The Vortex" that really makes a name for itself, with a powerful reef break coming off the harbour wall, famous among bodyboarders. Lifeguards are on patrol between 10am-6pm each day from mid-May to the last weekend of September. There is a seasonal dog ban in place at Portreath Beach from the 1st of July to the 31st of August, between 10am and 6pm. Dogs are welcome at all other times. The large beach has soft fine sand, with shingle below the shore line, that is popular with families. The white dome near Portreath is the radar itself, which provides long-range coverage of the south western approaches to the United Kingdom.

location: Kynance Cove, Cornwall, TR12 7PJ
notes: There is a seasonal dog ban in place from 1st July to 31st August, between the hours of 10am and 6pm. There are no lifeguards at this beach - visitors need to be aware of the tide to avoid getting cut off.

location: Carbis Bay Beach, St Ives, Cornwall, TR26 2NP
notes: Carbis Bay Beach is the winner of a Blue Flag Award and Seaside Award, which celebrates the commitment to environment, water quality, and safety of the beach. The bay’s lush cliffsides and position on the Atlantic Coast assure tranquil waters, making it the ideal spot for swimming. The history of Carbis Bay includes being formerly known as Barrepta Cove and hosting the 47th annual G7 summit in 2021. There is a seasonal dog ban in place at Carbis Bay Beach from the 15th of May to the 30th of September, between 10am and 6pm. Lifeguards are on patrol between 10am-6pm daily throughout the summer holiday. Car parking is available at the west end of the beach or at Porthrepta car park a few hundred yards away. The beach is open all year and is free for all visitors.

location: Bossiney Cove, Tintagel, Cornwall, PL34 0AX
notes: A small sheltered bay below the steep cliffs, it’s revealed only at low tide, as the beach opens and becomes one with neighbouring Benoath Cove. A tranquil sandy beach, it’s home to the distinctive rock formation known as Elephant Rock, spot it hidden in the cliff face or for those keen to explore further, discover the beach’s caverns. There is no lifeguard coverage.

location: Cawsand, Torpoint, Cornwall, PL10 1LE
notes: Dogs are welcome on this beach except between the 1 July - 31 August when a seasonal dog ban is in place between 10am and 6pm.

location: Great Western Beach, Newquay, Cornwall, TR7 2NE
notes: A section of Great Western has been cordoned off following cliff fall. Please be careful on the beach and stay away from the cordoned off area while inspections are carried out. Great Western Beach is a series of sandy coves that become a large golden expanse at low tide when the beach joins with neighbouring Tolcarne and Towan. Crooklets Beach has been awarded the Seaside Award which celebrates the commitment to environment, water quality, and safety of the beach. A popular beach for novice surfers, the beach benefits from the consistent Atlantic swell that gives Newquay its international reputation for good waves, whilst on shore, walkers, families and holidaymakers enjoy strolling along the sands, breathing in the salty sea air and exploring the caves and rock pools. The beach is reached either by walking along the sands at low tide or via a tarmaced path to the left of the Great Western Hotel. Lifeguards are stationed at the beach between 10am-6pm each day between 18th May and 29th September (2024). Dogs are allowed all year.

location: Gwynver Beach, Cornwall, TR19 7DG
notes: Gwynver Beach is a secluded stretch of golden sand to the north of Sennen Cove, named after King Arthur’s wife, Guinevere. It is an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty, surrounded by steep granite cliffs and accessible via an arduous path down through the sand dunes. The right hand side of the beach is dominated by the rocky headland of Aire Point, through which passes the South West Coast Path heading towards Cape Cornwall and providing spectacular views from the cliffs, and on fine days the Isles of Scilly. Providing some of the best surfing conditions in Cornwall, Gwynver attracts experienced locals with its ever present large waves. Life guards provide cover during the summer months and their advice should also be sought before going in the water. Lifeguard cover from May until September (2023). Parking: There's a small car park above the beach or at Sennen Cove.

location: Gunwalloe Church Cove Beach, Helston, Cornwall, TR12 7QG
notes: Gunwalloe Church Cove Beach on the Lizard Peninsula is so named because of the small medieval church that’s set into the rock of the headland on the north side of the beach. A National Trust owned beach and a site of archaeological and geological importance, its golden sand, grass-topped dunes and wildlife, attracts visitors from far and wide. The little church, St Wynwallow, has a uniquely detached bell tower, and was originally known as ‘Church of the Storms’ due to its exposed position on the eastern edge of Mounts Bay. Lovers of the Poldark TV series may recognise the beach as it featured in early episodes. The surf here is good, due to the Atlantic swell, although strong rip currents mean it’s not a beach for swimming and paddling. Lifeguards patrol the beach in the summer months. Please note: Dogs are welcome on this beach except in July and August when a seasonal dog ban is in place between 10am and 6pm.

location: Crooklets Beach, Bude, Cornwall, EX23 8LE
notes: Crooklets Beach on the north coast of Cornwall offers a wide expanse of golden sand that’s exposed at low tide and bordered by rocky outcrops ideal for rock-pooling. As of 2024, Crooklets Beach has been awarded both the Blue Flag and the Seaside Award. On the northern edge of the seaside town of Bude, which first became popular with Victorian holidaymakers during the 19th century, Crooklets Beach is just a short walk from the town centre. The beach has great facilities including a large car park, level access and viewing area, a play area, skate park, beach cafe, showers, amusements and pubs close by. It has lifeguards from mid-May to the last weekend of September. A sand chair is available for disabled visitors. Dogs are not allowed on the beach between 10am-6pm from the 15th May to 30th September. Dogs are welcome on the beach the rest of the year.

location: Helford Passage Beach, Helford, Cornwall, TR11 5LB
notes: The Helford is one of the most picturesque estuaries in Cornwall and this shingle and sand beach is situated in an unspoilt sheltered bay beside the popular 300-year-old Ferry Boat Inn. The small beach is accessible at low tide and is located on the north side of the estuary where the passenger ferry crosses the river to the small village of Helford on the south side. A popular launching place for motor boats and small yachts, hire a boat from the village or set out on the South West Coast Path that passes nearby on a wonderful walk eastwards along the estuary towards the sub-tropical gardens at Glendurgan and Trebah.

location: Gorran Haven, St Austell, Cornwall, PL26 6JG
notes: This beach is dog friendly, however they must be kept on leads. Nearby, The Dodman headland, with its Iron Age hillfort is well worth exploring. The annual swim takes locals on a 3.8km journey out and around the rocks and back to the beach. The Gwineas, fifteen rocks that are a haven for seals and cormorants, are off the coast. Dolphins are often seen swimming near them.

location: Hayle Towans Beach, Hayle, Cornwall, TR27 4DE
notes: Hayle Towans Beach is a vast expanse of golden sand backed by sand dunes and is the beginning of Hayle’s ‘Three Mile Beach’ within St Ives Bay, joining with neighbouring bays, Gwithian and Godrevy, at low tide. The village of Phillack lies half a mile inland behind the dunes and is a Site of Special Scientific Importance, it’s also home to the shockingly named pub, the Bucket of Blood. Legend tells, during its smuggling days, of a murdered customs officer that was found at the bottom of the well.

location: Crantock, Newquay, Cornwall, TR8 5SE
notes: Visitors are asked to take extra care around the dune system at Crantock Beach. Please stay clear from the base of the sand cliffs and stay on the paths through the dunes. Do not breach fenced off areas. Crantock beach’s large expanse of golden sands and dramatic grass-topped dunes sit between the cliffs of thet Pentire headlands, whilst the Gannel river flows into the sea from the east. Just a 15-minute drive from the bustling town of Newquay, this National Trust owned beach remains surprisingly quiet even during the summer months and is a perfect spot for swimming, surfing, and snorkelling, or wild walks year-round. Cafes, toilets and parking with 150 spaces are nearby, along with a camping site. To access the beach, please use the level path from the right hand corner of the National Trust car park. RNLI Lifeguard cover from May until September. The RNLI strongly advise that visitors should only swim when lifeguards are on duty and obey the flags that are put up on the beach showing where and when it is safe to enter the water. The River Gannel causes currents that can be dangerous, in particular at certain stages of the tide. The lifeguards advise not swimming near the river flow and only when and where they designate it is safe to do so. Dog friendly, but please keep dogs under control.

location: Harlyn Bay Beach, Padstow, Cornwall, PL28 8SQ
notes: Lifeguards are on the beach from May until September and then weekends until October half-term, when they will be in place all week. (2022) Surfing Information: When the swell is big on the west facing beaches and the wind is from a southwest direction, Harlyn will be the best wave around. The horseshoe shaped bay produces waves from low through to high providing rights off a rock at the east end of the beach - fast and sucky waves with a ledgy take off, to a peak in the middle producing lefts and rights which are hollow and fast. Harlyn Surf School offer a choice of fantastic activities, surfing, coasteering, stand up paddleboarding and guided sit on top kayak tours. plus Multi activity days, all based at Harlyn Bay.
A dog ban is in place all year long

location: Constantine Bay, Padstow, Cornwall, PL28 8JH
notes: Lifeguards man the beach daily from 1st May – 26th September and also over weekends from Easter to the end of October (2022).

location: Daymer Bay Beach, Rock, Cornwall, PL27 6LA
notes: A stunning beach that at low tide forms long stretches of golden sand backed by dunes all the way around to Rock, with superb views across the Camel Estuary. Perfect for families. A sheltered bay within the Camel Estuary, its clear waters make it a haven for swimming and paddling, but also for kitesurfing, being an ideal spot for beginners. For far-reaching views climb Brea Hill at the end of the beach or walk to the charming St Enodoc Church, a picture-perfect chapel with Saxon heritage that sits amongst the sand dunes, and the resting place of former poet laureate Sir John Betjeman.

location: Housel Bay Beach, Lizard, Helston, TR12 7PG
notes: Dogs are welcome on this beach except during July and August (10am - 6pm) when a seasonal dog ban is in place.

location: Chapel Porth Beach, St Agnes, Cornwall, TR5 0NT
notes: Dogs are welcome on this beach except in July and August when a seasonal dog ban is in place between 10am and 6pm. Lifeguard cover from May to September. Car park free to National Trust members. No overnight camping allowed. The dramatic ruins of the old Wheal Coates tin mine are perched on the cliffs above the beach, and the walk from there around the coast to the village of St Agnes gives stunning views. Seasonal beach cafe and ice cream kiosk. The cafe just up from the beach where in winter sipping a hot chocolate and watching the ocean is a popular pastime, as is tucking in to the café’s legendary 'hedgehog' ice creams, a concoction of Cornish ice cream, covered in clotted cream and topped with crushed hazelnuts.

location: Downderry Beach, Downderry, Looe, Cornwall, PL11 3JR
notes: Downderry Beach is a long, expansive grey sand and shingle beach about five miles east of Looe. It is backed by a sea wall that leads to the nearby Seaton village and beach. The sheltered beach which is dog-friendly throughout the year is popular for swimming, fishing, and snorkeling, whilst at low tide the beach’s biodiverse rock pools are exposed, ready for exploration. For walkers the South West Coast Path runs through Downderry (officially along the road through the village, though most people use the seawall that is much safer!) and it is also possible to walk on along the beach going east towards Batten Cliffs. However, there is no safe access back up the cliffs to the coast path and you may discover the nearby (unofficial) naturist beach. The village of Downderry has a small general store, a pub and a café.

location: Eastern Green, Penzance, Cornwall
notes: Eastern Green beach is the closest to the historic port town of Penzance, a lovely local beach with a long stretch of sand and shingle bordering Mount Bay. It is a clean and sheltered haven with gently sloping shelf and large area of shallow waters, perfect for keen paddlers or young explorers. Dogs are allowed on Eastern Green beach all year round, but there are summer dog bans on Longrock Beach. The beach is best accessed from the South West Coast Path.

location: Hannafore Beach, Looe, Cornwall, PL13 2DG
notes: Hannafore Beach is a quiet, shingle beach with some sandy stretches and plenty of rock pools at low tide. It is a quieter alternative from its bustling sandy neighbour at East Looe and popular with dog walkers year-round. With its long walkable sea wall, Hannafore is accessible to many. There's free parking on the road above and two seasonally open cafes, a putting green, tennis courts and from here you can start the walk along the South West Coast Path to Polperro, about five miles away. Just off the coast is Looe Island, a marine nature reserve and accessible by boat from the harbour. Hannafore is famed for its rockpooling with easy access to large shallow pools full of starfish, crabs and prawns. The local Marine Conservation group operate regular rockpools rambles throughout the year.

location: Duckpool Beach, Bude, Cornwall, EX23 9HW
notes: Duckpool Beach in North Cornwall is a wild and untamed pebble and rock-lined beach with a sandy shoreline that’s exposed at low tide. This stunning National Trust owned beach four miles north of Bude is where the beautiful wooded Coombe Valley meets the sea; its woodland covered in lichens whilst its floor is carpeted in maritime grasses and wild flowers. Here too, the spectacular 100-metre-high Steeple Point Cliff dominates the beach. Anti-tank blocks installed before WW2 can be found scattered along the beach. This spectacularly wild area of coast is notorious for shipwrecks and not suitable for swimming due to its dangerous currents. There's a National Trust car park, free to members, No overnight camping allowed. Dogs allowed all year round, but please keep under control.

location: Hawker's Cove Beach, Padstow, Cornwall, PL28 8HW
notes: Hawkers Cove beach is off the beaten track and offers a change of pace away from the bustling fishing harbour of Padstow. It is best reached on foot along the South West Coast Path from the town. There's a small tea shop here but little else. Hawkers Cove was previously the location of the RNLI Padstow Lifeboat Station, but it's now far too shallow even at high tide to launch from here, the result of the sands shifting over the years. On the way to the delightful little sandy cove, the coastal footpath passes Gun Point, where you’ll find abandoned fortifications dating back to the Napoleonic war. Opposite are the golden sands of Daymer Bay and when the tide comes in, part of the beach is submerged to form the infamous Doom Bar sand bank that has been a perilous hazard to shipping for centuries.

location: Gwithian Towans Beach, Hayle, Cornwall, TR27 5BX
notes: Gwithian Towans is a vast and beautifully rugged sandy beach that forms part of Three Mile Beach within St Ives Bay. Towans is the Cornish word for ‘sand dunes,' and these golden hills tufted with wild grass, alongside dramatic cliffs are the backdrop to a shore shaped by the Atlantic swell and often swept by a strong sea breeze making it a favourite for surfers and kite surfers for the consistent year-round swell. At low tide the large areas of rock pools are uncovered around Strap Rocks, just waiting to be explored and keen eyes should look out for resident grey seals often spotted off the coastline.

location: Coverack Beach, The Lizard, Cornwall, TR12 6SP
notes: Coverack beach is dog friendly, but dogs must be kept on leads during June, July and August (2023). There is also a small rocky beach at Perprean Cove to the south of the village.

Lifeguard cover on Fistral Beach from the Easter until the end of October. Lifeguard cover on South Fistral Beach from the 10th of July until the 5th of September (2022). Sand chairs are available from Fistral Surf Hire Shop. Telephone: [01637850584] (Tel:01637850584). Sand chairs are provided by Cornwall Mobility in partnership with Disability Cornwall and Isles of Scilly.

location: Hemmick Beach, Veryan, Cornwall, TR2 5QA
notes: A peaceful and secluded bay, Hemmick is a beautiful sandy south-west facing beach surrounded by rolling pasture and dramatic rocky headlands. The small unspoilt cove is considered a ‘secret beach,’ and can only be accessed by a steep narrow road from Boswinger, near Gorran Haven. It’s wild and untamed, with plenty of tiny coves and rock pools to explore at low tide. Less than a mile away, take a wander up to The Dodman, one of the highest headlands on the south Cornish coast. There's the remains of an Iron Age fortification and a seven meter high granite cross erected in the late 1800s.

location: Charlestown Beach, Charlestown, St Austell, Cornwall, PL25 3NJ
notes: Dogs are not allowed on the beaches from 1st April to 31st October, but welcome the rest of the time.

location: Mullion Cove beach, Mullion, Cornwall, TR12 7EP
notes: Mullion Cove on the west coast of the Lizard Peninsula is a small sandy beach, mostly covered at high tide, beside the historic lifeboat station and picturesque Mullion harbour. The small Victorian harbour originally built in the 1890s sits along an unspoilt coastline of rugged headlands and small islands, the largest, Mullion Island – an uninhabited sanctuary to for nesting seabirds. The small quay remains a working harbour today and protects a fleet of small boats from the full force of the Atlantic.

location: Pentewan Beach, West End, Pentewan, St Austell, Cornwall, PL26 6BX
notes: Pentewan Beach stretches for over a half a mile, it’s east-facing sheltered bay, white shingly sand and clear waters inviting beachgoers to swim, surf, paddle, and play. Like most Cornish beaches, the views from the shore of Pentewan are spectacular, with rolling headlands framing its vast shoreline. Backed by a large holiday park, the beach is very family friendly but never feels too crowded. Just set back from the sea, the village of Pentewan was once a bustling port for both fishing and exporting tin and china clay. The old harbour remains, but with a silted up entrance can no longer be reached from the sea. The former railway line that stretched from here to St Austell is now a popular walking and cycle path. Please note The beach is privately owned and the owners have the right to say when dogs can go on the beach. They may change this policy at any time, therefore please check direct with the holiday park.

location: Mousehole, Penzance, TR19 6QG
notes: Dogs are welcome on the beach except for July and August, when there is a seasonal ban in place between 10am and 6pm.

location: Bude, Cornwall, EX23 9EL
notes: Northcott Mouth is a rocky cove on the north coast that reveals a sandy shore and scattered rock pools at low tide, overlooked by untamed Cornish wildflower-topped cliffs. Children will delight in the little stream crossing the beach and the rock pools, while surfers will enjoy the waves created by rocky reefs offshore. The National Trust have a small car park adjacent to the beach. Northcott Mouth is steeped in history, with nearby Bronze Age burial chambers found at Maer Cliff, and the wreck of the SS Belem, which can be seen at low tide. Wrecked in November 1917, the propeller shaft was salvaged and used as a metal support for Barrel Rock at the end of Bude Breakwater. There are no toilet facilities. In the summer months, there is a delightful tea caravan with rustic garden set back from the beach. Lifeguard Cover is available in summer months. Dogs are welcome.

location: Polurrian Cove, Mullion, Cornwall TR12 7EN
notes: Polurrian Cove is a sandy west-facing beach within walking distance of Mullion, the largest village on the Lizard Peninsula. It is owned by Polurrian on the Lizard and can be accessed through the hotel grounds. Set in a designated Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty and a Site of Special Scientific Interest (SSSI), Polurrian Cove’s vast shoreline of golden sand and patches of fine shingle are revealed at low tide. Surrounded by imposing wild Cornish cliffs and rugged rocky bluffs, the beach is exposed to Atlantic swell for good surf. If you prefer to stay on shore, the South West Coast Path will lead you over the undulating headlands to Mullion Cove or to the famous Poldhu Cove and the Lizard Wireless Telegraph Station, where Italian inventor, Guglielmo Marconi, sent the first transatlantic radio signal from in December 1901. LIFEGUARD PATROL TIMES 2024: Weekends and Bank Holidays Only 13 July-01 September Patrol times 10am-6pm Polurrian Cove has a dog ban from 1st July to 31st August between 10am - 6pm and is dog friendly outside these hours and from 1st September to 30th June (2024).

location: Kenneggy Sands Beach, Nr Marazion, Cornwall, TR20 9AU
notes: Kenneggy Sands is a beautifully secluded and unspoilt bay between Helston and Penzance that can only be reached at low tide. Access the bay via the South West Coast Path from either the popular coastal village of Praa Sands or Prussia Cove. An area rich in smuggling history, pass bricked up cellars that were once used by notorious smugglers, the Carter brothers, whilst the quaint cottages you pass are said to have been built to prevent their activities. When revealed by the tide, this stretch of golden sand is fringed with a rocky outcrop and overlooked by imposing wildflower and heath-covered cliffs.

location: Longrock Beach, Penzance, Cornwall TR20 9BJ
notes: Dogs are not allowed on the beach east of the level crossing during July and August (between the hours of 10am - 6pm) when a seasonal dog ban is in place.

location: Lamorna Cove Beach, Penzance, Cornwall, TR19 6XH
notes: The cove lies on the South West Coast Path between Porthcurno and Mousehole. A nice quiet spot for swimming and popular with scuba divers. There is no lifeguard cover provided and no public toilets. There is a seasonal café and, further up the valley, a pub. Please be aware the car park at the cove is privately owned, and is monitored by ANPR (Automatic Number Plate Recognition) cameras. The parking payment machines are cash only.

location: Mexico Towans Beach, Hayle, Cornwall, TR27 5AG
notes: Mexico Towans Beach forms part of a breath-taking three miles of golden sand that starts from the mouth of the Hayle estuary and reaches out towards the lighthouse at Godrevy Point. This remote and untamed stretch of beach situated between Hayle and Gwithian, is backed by magnificent sand dunes known as 'towans.' Mexico Towans beach is a Site of Special Scientific Interest (SSSI); nationally important for wildlife, the landscape allows about 300 different plants to occur within the dunes, which are Cornwall’s second largest sand dune ecosystem, spreading for approximately 400 hectares and made up from wind-blown, lime-rich shell sand.

location: Pendower Beach, Cornwall, TR2 5LW
notes: Pendower Beach is a National Trust owned beach located within Gerrans Bay and overlooked by Nare Head to the east. It joins with Carne at low tide to form over a mile of golden shoreline. The beach is backed by low soft cliffs and rock pools designated as Sites of Special Scientific Interest (SSSI's) due to the area’s biodiverse geology and wildlife. The pretty village of Veryan, with its thatched round houses, is about a mile inland, and the five star Nare Hotel overlooks the beach, offering afternoon teas on the lawns.

location: Lansallos Beach, Polperro, Cornwall, PL13 2QU
notes: The beach has no facilities. Please keep dogs under control.

location: Lusty Glaze Beach Road, Newquay, Cornwall TR7 3AE
notes: Lusty Glaze is a privately owned sandy beach on the edge of Newquay; a secluded cove, it’s relatively sheltered by the imposing high cliffs which form a natural amphitheater. Open to the public at no cost and dog-friendly all year-round, steep steps take you down onto the golden sands of the beach, whilst at the heart of the Lusty Glaze bay is a relaxed and friendly bar and restaurant, with breath-taking views and sunsets year-round. The Lusty Glaze Adventure Centre offers a range of adrenalin-fuelled activities on the shore, on the cliff and in the water, from climbing and abseiling and ‘Terror Tight Ropes’ to jet skiing and banana-boating. Lifeguard cover from the July until September (2023).

location: Kingsand Beach, Torpoint, Cornwall, PL10 1NA
notes: There is currently a discussion about banning dogs on the beach in summer months, so please check when you visit (Feb 2023)

location: Polridmouth Cove Beach, Fowey, Cornwall, PL23 1EB
notes: Polridmouth Cove Beach is a quiet sheltered cove to the west of Fowey, separating into two small bays at high tide by a low rocky outcrop. The only way to get there is on foot, which preserves its seclusion. The beach is shrouded in history, from its intriguing seawater bath built into the rocks by the Rashleigh family, to the 1920s ornamental lakes that back the beach. These were used in WW2 as decoy sites, complete with dams and lights, to imitate the nearby Fowey harbour. Most famously though, Polridmouth inspired the author Daphne du Maurier, who featured the beach in her 1938 gothic novel, Rebecca, long before she lived at the nearby Menabilly House. From Fowey the South West Coast Path passes this serene cove before climbing up to Gribben Head with its iconic red and white tower, offering walkers stunning Cornish coastal views from Fowey to St Austell.

location: Poldhu Cove Beach, Mullion, Cornwall, TR12 7HZ
notes: Dogs are welcome on this beach except between 1 July and 31 August (10am - 6pm) when a seasonal dog ban is in place. The Marconi Centre at Poldhu is located on the cliff top south of the beach and operated by volunteers at Poldhu Amateur Radio Club.

location: Par Sands Beach, St Austell, Cornwall, PL25 5DS
notes: Par Sands Beach is a wide sandy expanse backed by low dunes close to the village of Par, just four miles from the town of St Austell. Southwesterly winds make Par Sands a good kite-surfing and windsurfing beach, whilst it’s also a popular dog-walking beach year-round.

location: Nansidwell Beach, Falmouth, Cornwall, TR11 5HN
notes: A quiet secluded cove to the west of historic Falmouth, Nansidwell Beach, also known as ‘Woodlands,’ is a small, sand and shingle bay concealed by a beautiful woodland. Situated between Maenporth and Mawnan Smith, this privately owned beach is a welcome slice of calm away from busier bays. Follow the footpath through a lovely woodland area, partly cared for by the National Trust and down to the bay for snorkelling, diving, swimming, or just relaxing on the golden sands. It’s a dog-friendly beach, but please be aware of other people on the beach and take any waste away with you.

location: TR12 7LT
notes: Dogs are welcome on this beach except during July and August (10am - 6pm) when a seasonal dog ban is in place.

location: Maenporth Beach, Falmouth, Cornwall, TR11 5HN
notes: Dogs are welcome on this beach except during July and August (10am to 6pm) when a seasonal dog ban is in place. The gently sloping beach of Maenporth was once a natural harbour but today the shallow inlet is an ideal spot for young swimmers, paddlers, and kayaks, whilst at low tide the rock pools are plenty. There are excellent family facilities that include a cafe, car parking, public toilets and the opportunity to hire out a range of watersports activities including kayaking, sailing and scuba diving. The shipwreck of the 'Ben Asdale' can be spotted off shore, and is often explored by divers. There is no RNLI Beach Lifeguard presence on the beach.

location: Marazion Beach, Marazion, Cornwall, TR17 0EN
notes: Dogs are not allowed on this beach during July and August (between the hours of 10am - 6pm) when a seasonal dog ban is in place. (2023) Lifeguard cover from the 8th of July until the 3rd of September (2023).

location: Mawgan Porth, Newquay, Cornwall, TR8 4DA
notes: Full lifeguard cover from the 29th April until the 24th of September (2023). Then weekends throughout October and all of October half-term.

location: Lantic Bay, Polperro, Cornwall, PL13 2QU
notes: Lantic Bay is the definition of a ‘hidden gem;’ within an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty, it’s crystal-clear waters, white sand and shingle shoreline, backed by imposing cliffs are the reward for taking on the challenging steep and rocky terrain. A peaceful haven owned by the National Trust, this beautiful cove between Fowey and Polperro is unspoilt and its remoteness means it's never crowded. There's a National Trust car park on the road to Polruan, or you can walk along the South West Coast Path. Caution is advised for swimmers, as there can be a strong rip in the bay and the beach shelves dramatically at times. Access to the beach is across fields and then down a steep rocky path to the beach. It is not suitable for buggys. There are no lifeguards, toilets or refreshments.

location: Perranuthnoe Beach, Penzance, Cornwall, TR20 9LZ
notes: Dogs are welcome on this beach except between 1st July and 31st August (10am - 6pm) when a seasonal dog ban is in place.

location: Loe Bar Beach, Cornwall, TR13 9DZ
notes: Loe Bar beach is a half mile sand and shingle bank that separates The Loe, Cornwall’s largest natural freshwater lake, from the sea. Within an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty, Loe Bar beach originally formed the mouth of the river Cober which led to a harbour in Helston. However, by the 13th century the bar had cut Helston off from the sea and formed The Loe. Not considered safe for swimming due to its strong currents, Loe Bar beach is popular amongst cyclists and walkers. It’s dog-friendly year-round and can be accessed via the South West Coast Path from Porthleven or from Helston, where bike hire is also available.

location: Porthchapel Beach, St Levan, Nr Porthcurno, Cornwall, TR19 7AA
notes: From the 1st of May to 30th September (8am to 7pm) dogs are not allowed below the mean high tide line, but they are allowed all year above the mean high tide line.

location: Portheras Cove, St Just, Cornwall, TR19 7DN
notes: Please note, the cliff-face along Portheras Cove Beach is unstable and the beach has experienced rockfall in recent months. Visitors are required to be extra cautious and under no circumstances should people sit under and near the cliffs. Lifeguard cover: There is no lifeguard presence at Portheras Cove Beach. The beach does not have any public facilities including toilets and bins. Please respect the beach and take all litter and belongings away with you at the end of your visit. This secret cove, often visited by seals, is on Cornwall’s wild Tin Coast and is an SSSI designated area, so visitors are asked to respect all wildlife and make sure to keep a distance from wild visitors to the cove. Isolated and only accessible on foot, the South West Coast Path passes above it with steep rocky steps leading down past a waterfall onto the beach. The iconic Pendeen Lighthouse, built in 1891, has parking beside it from where you can walk to the beach. There is no mobile or wifi signal on the beach.

location: Porthleven Beach, Helston, Cornwall, TR13 9EN
notes: Porthleven Beach is three glorious miles of golden sand and steeply shelving shingle running east from the historic harbour. A rough and dangerous stretch of sea, it’s reportedly the reason why the harbour, the most southerly port in the UK, was built in the early 1800s. A refuge on the wild Cornish coast and an area once notorious for shipwrecks. It’s not recommended to swim along this beach, but when the tide is out, you can walk along the vast shoreline to Loe Bar, Cornwall’s largest freshwater lake. RNLI Lifeguards patrol the beach during the summer months.

location: St Ives, Cornwall, TR26 1LG
notes: Dogs are welcome on this beach except between the 1st July and the 31st August (10am - 6pm) when a seasonal dog ban is in place. (2023)

location: Porth Joke Beach, known locally as ‘Polly Joke’
notes: Porth Joke Beach, known locally as ‘Polly Joke’ is an archetypal Cornish bay of wild rocky outcrops, a sandy beach, undulating headlands, turquoise sea, and craggy cliff-faces. This small but beautiful north-west facing cove is owned and cared for by the National Trust and is a walk away from any parking, attracting only the keenest of beachgoers and explorers. Walking the South West Coast Path is a popular pastime amongst these bays that boast a feeling of total remoteness that entices you to explore every inlet for fear of missing out on the most beautiful views. Originally the bay was called ‘Pol Lejouack,’ meaning ‘Jackdaw Cove’ supposedly sounding a little like “Polly Joke.”

location: Porthgwidden Beach, St Ives, Cornwall, TR26 1PL
notes: Dogs are welcome on this beach except from the 1st July to the 31st August between 10am and 6pm when a seasonal dog ban is in place (2023).

location: Porth Kidney Sands, St Ives, Cornwall, TR26 3GN
notes: The beach is dog friendly all year. However, dogs are required to be kept on a lead on the footpath leading from St Uny Church to Porth Kidney Sands. (St Ives Town Council) Lifeguard cover from the 8th of July until the 3rd of September (2023). Swimming should not be undertaken in and around the mouth of the Hayle Estuary. The beach is backed by picturesque sand dunes and the West Cornwall Golf Club, said to be the oldest golf club in Cornwall. There’s no parking close to the beach and no facilities. Access is on foot via the South West Coast Path from St Uny Church or Lelant Railway Station and does involve steps. The neighbouring Carbis Bay sits the other side of the Carrack Gladden headland and is a short walk away along the South West Coast Path which runs behind the beach.

location: Seaton Beach, Nr Looe, Cornwall, PL13 1PX
notes: Seaton Beach in south east Cornwall offers a large expanse of sand and small pebbles cut through by the river Seaton. A family-favourite, it's great for paddling and play, with easy access, and plenty of parking. The beach is very popular with dog walkers, shore fisherman, and is one of the few beaches in this part of Cornwall that provides good waves for surfing. There's a selection of cafe's and a pub for refreshments. Behind the beach, is the Seaton Valley Country Park, home to an abundance of wildlife such as dragonflies, butterflies, ducks, kingfishers, dormice, and otters. The main path is flat and takes you deep into the valley. Lifeguards patrol the beach between May and September. RNLI; Seaton Beach

location: Porthluney Cove Beach, Caerhays, Mevagissey, Cornwall, PL26 6LY
notes: The beach is directly in front of the daily charge car park where you will also find a range of seasonal pop-up cafes, a picnic area and toilets. The beach is dog friendly all year round but visitors are requested to keep their dogs on leads from April-October. There is no Lifeguard cover provided.

location: Porth Beach, Newquay, Cornwall TR7 3NH
notes: Lifeguards are on patrol between 10am-6pm each day between 18th May to 29th September. (2024) Dogs are banned from the beach between 1st July and 31st August, between the hours of 10am and 6pm. Dogs are welcome at all other times.

location: Porthminster Beach, St Ives, Cornwall, TR26 2BN
notes: Lifeguards are on patrol between 10am-6pm each day between 18th May to 29th September. (2024) Dogs are banned from the beach between May 15th and September 30th, between the hours of 10am and 6pm. Dogs are welcome at all other times. Sand chairs provided by Cornwall Mobility in partnership with Disability Cornwall and Isles of Scilly may be available from Porthminster Beach Cafe. Telephone: 01736 795352

location: TR19 7NN
notes: Priest Cove is a small fishing bay with a quaint slipway, located in the crook of the Cape, overlooked by its imposing cliffs. A small man-made tidal pool has been built amongst the rocks. Offshore, the Brisons Rocks, known affectionately as 'General de Gaulle in his bath', provide a sanctuary for many types of seabirds.

location: Readymoney Cove Beach, Fowey, Cornwall, PL23 1EB
notes: Dogs are welcome on this beach except between July 1st and August 31st (10am-6pm) when a seasonal dog ban is in place. (2023) There's a small cafe/shop and toilets.

location: Portscatho Beach, Portscatho, The Roseland, Cornwall, TR2 5LW
notes: Dogs are welcome on this beach except between 1st July and 31st August (10am-6pm) when a seasonal dog ban is in place. (2023)

location: Porthcurnick Beach, Portscatho, The Roseland, Cornwall, TR2 5EW
notes: Porthcurnick is a beautiful south-east facing sandy cove on the beautiful, unspoilt Roseland Peninsula and within Cornwall’s Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty. A National Trust owned beach, Porthcurnick is just north of Portscatho, and a favourite for families and visitors for its biodiverse and thriving rock pools, as well as the easy access to water activities via the beach’s slipway.

location: Porthpean Beach, St Austell, Cornwall, PL25 3RD
notes: Dogs are welcome on this beach except between July 1st and 31st August (10am-6pm) when a seasonal dog ban is in place. (2023) Access to the beach is on a steep incline from the privately run car park.

location: Portwrinkle Beach, Crafthole, Nr. Torpoint, Cornwall, PL11 3BP
notes: Dogs are not allowed on the beach during July and August, between the hours of 10am and 6pm.

location: Rock, Nr Padstow, Cornwall, PL28 8QL
notes: Rock beach is a vast stretch of golden sands and turquoise sea on the shore of the Camel Estuary, opposite the popular town of Padstow on Cornwall’s north coast. A breath-taking shoreline, the long sandy beach that fronts the village of Rock is a favourite spot for swimmers and sun-seekers, whilst offshore the Camel Estuary lures sailors, wind surfers and kite surfers to enjoy the strong sea breeze. From Rock beach there are far-reaching along the wide estuary; within an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty, Rock and the surrounding coast is a wildlife-watchers haven, whilst walkers delight in the coastal routes across the sand to Daymer Bay and Polzeath. A small ferry from Rock makes the short trip over to Padstow, for those looking to wander around one of Cornwall’s most iconic finishing harbours. This sandy beach, with stunning views of the Camel Estuary, is perfect for families and their four-legged friends. With St Michael's Church and Porthilly Beach Holiday Park, it offers a great base for your stay, where you can explore the scenic coastal paths and surrounding dunes.

location: Port Gaverne, Cornwall, PL29 3RH
notes: Port Gaverne is a sheltered, narrow cove with plenty of sand at low tide and near neighbour to Port Isaac. Some claim it may be the quaintest cove in North Cornwall? A National Trust owned beach which has remained almost unchanged in hundreds of years is popular with families as it has plenty of rock pools. Once a thriving port landing slate and coal and also a busy fishing port for pilchards. The origin of the name Gaverne is thought to have come from 'Karn Hun' meaning rocky haven and is still spelt 'Port Gavern' by a few locals - pronounced 'gay-verne'. Fans of Doc Martin may recognise the cove as it has appeared several times in the tv programme over the years.

location: Porthoustock Beach, St Keverne, The Lizard, Cornwall, TR12 7NQ
notes: Porthoustock Beach, known locally as ‘Pro'stock,’ is an east-facing pebble beach with a large expanse of coarse grey sand and shingle revealed at low tide, and a popular area for divers with many shipwrecks to be explored around the treacherous reef, The Manacles. This sheltered bay on the eastern side of the Lizard Peninsula has been a quarry and shipping port for stone since the 1890s; evident by the overshadowing concrete silo, once used to store aggregate, that now sits disused at the end of the beach, whilst at the other end, there is a quay which was used to load the stone onto the boats. Swimming should be done with care. Parking is allowed at the back of the beach taking care not to obstruct the boats of the local fishermen. There are toilets behind the beach and some picturesque thatched cottages.

location: Sandymouth Beach, Bude, Cornwall, EX23 9HW
notes: Sandymouth Beach is an untouched pebble and sand beach on the wild north coast. A waterfall interrupts the imposing sea-beaten cliffs of this rugged beach, known for its fascinating geology. An unspoilt stretch of sand owned and cared for by the National Trust, the beach widens at low tide, revealing rock pools along the shore, that spans almost 2 miles to join with neighbouring bays like Crooklets. A Site of Special Scientific Interest (SSSI) for its geological features including fossilised plant remains and 300-million-year-old twisted rock formations. Lifeguards patrol the beach in summer months.

location: Praa Sands Beach, Penzance, Cornwall, TR20 9TQ
notes: Full lifeguard cover will resume from 29th of April to 24th of September. Weekend cover will remain from 30th of September to 15th of October, with half-term cover from 21st to 29th of October. Patrol times are between 10am and 6pm. (2023) Please note: Dogs are welcome on this beach except between July 1st and August 31st (10am - 6pm) when a seasonal dog ban is in place. (2023) The beach’s geological features have also gained it recognition as a Regionally Important Geological and Geomorphological Site (RIGS), after erosion exposed a thin layer of 2000 year-old peat once buried deep below the sand dunes.

location: Portholland Beach, Portholland, The Roseland, Cornwall, TR2 5QA
notes: Portholland Beach is made up of two small, secluded coves of grey stone and rocky outcrops. Backed by a granite sea wall that protects the tiny hamlets of East and West Portholland, home to around forty residents. At low tide the coves join to become a wide stretch of unspoilt sandy shoreline, just one of many secluded spots along the Roseland that have remained largely unchanged for over a century. The Roseland Peninsula is part of Cornwall's National Landscape, formerly known as an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty, and boasts unrivalled scenery and a relatively mild climate year-round.

location: Porthcothan Bay Beach, Padstow, Cornwall, PL28 8LW
notes: Lifeguard cover from the 13th of May until the 24th of September (2023). You are advised to always check beach conditions before your visit and always follow the lifeguards advice whilst on the beach. Porthcothan is a dog friendly beach, with no seasonal dog ban, but please keep your dog under control and clean up mess immediately. Poldark connection: Porthcothan Beach and the clifftop fields nearby were used for the filming of Poldark, especially the shots of Ross riding his horse.

location: Trebarwith Strand, Tintagel, Cornwall, PL34 0HB
notes: Trebarwith Strand is an archetypal north coast beach; wild and untamed, its a mile-long stretch of golden sand and rocky outcrops only revealed at low tide. Located just over two miles south-west of the historical village of Tintagel, this dog-friendly beach at the base of imposing weather-beaten cliffs, welcomes walkers, wildlife watchers and explorers to enjoy the sea breeze year-round. With Gull Rock just off the coast being a sanctuary for sea birds, an abundance of biodiversity in its rock pools and far-reaching coastal views from the coastal path, this peaceful bay is one for nature lovers and visitors looking to avoid the crowds. Swimming is only recommended when there are lifeguards on watch due to dangerous currents.

location: Treyarnon Bay, Padstow, Cornwall, PL28 8JR
notes: Treyarnon Bay between Padstow and Mawgan Porth is a lovely clean, north-west facing, sandy beach surrounded by low cliffs and backed by sand dunes. The dramatic cliffs, turquoise waters, and golden sands of Treyarnon Bay are striking rain or shine, and are sheltered somewhat by neighbouring beaches, inviting walkers, surfers, and families year-round. The South West Coast Path runs right across the sand and back up the headland, providing the perfect spot for hikers to rest weary legs, as well as non-stop views around every bluff. It’s also a popular family beach for its expanse of fine sand at low water, biodiverse rock pools and its natural 8ft deep tidal pool, whilst surfers can take advantage of consistent left and right hand waves.

location: Upton Towans Beach, Hayle, Cornwall, TR27 5AX
notes: Upton Towans beach is situated to the north of Hayle and is the middle section of the three mile long stretch of beach on the eastern side of St Ives Bay. It's ideal for surfing and safe for bathing and backed by sand dunes (known as towans in Cornwall) and adjacent holiday camping sites. Lifeguard cover from the 13th of May until the 24th of September (2023). Dogs allowed all year round.

location: Tolcarne Beach, Newquay, Cornwall, TR7 1AF
notes: Tolcarne Beach’s soft golden sand bay is overlooked by Newquay’s dramatic sea cliffs, joining up with its neighbouring beaches Great Western and Lusty Glaze at low tide. The beautiful crescent bay near the centre of the popular Cornish town offers far-reaching scenic views of the surrounding headlands, whilst offshore, there’s easy swimming and family surfing to be had, and exciting rock pools to explore at low tide. It’s also a popular spot for sea fishing and home of the famed 'Tolcarne Wedge' a heavy wave enjoyed by bodyboarders, that breaks towards the breakwater then rebounds to form the distinctive "Tolcarne Wedge."

location: Widemouth Bay, Bude, Cornwall, EX23 0AW
notes: Widemouth Bay is a wild and wide sandy bay stretching for nearly 2 miles. Exposed to the full fury of the Atlantic with large rocky outcrops at either end, it’s a favourite surf spot. Situated just 3 miles south of the seaside town of Bude and accessible along the South West Coast Path, Widemouth Bay offers unrivalled scenery, and ideal conditions to learn to surf or body-board. At the southern end of the beach the shore becomes very rocky; known as Blackrock Beach, there is an abundance of rock pools and it's home to array of biodiverse marine life and the distinctive formation ‘Black Rock,’ which rises above the rest. The beach is additionally patrolled in the Easter school holidays and October half-term. As well as weekends between 20th April - 28th April and 5th October and 20th October. (2024) Dogs are banned from the beach between May 15th and September 30th, between the hours of 10am and 6pm. Dogs are welcome at all other times.

location: Trevaunance Cove Beach, St Agnes, Cornwall, TR5 0RU
notes: Trevaunance Cove is the main beach near the small village of St Agnes, along the St Agnes Heritage Coast and a best kept Cornish secret. It’s a wild and rugged cliffs overlook the sandy cove in this Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty, contrasted with the quaint village houses that lead to the shore of crystal-clear sea. The remains of the old harbour can be explored on the western side of the beach at low tide, and you can walk to the neighbouring northerly beach of Trevellas Porth, with plenty rocks to climb over and rock pools to discover. Historically, village’s rich mineral deposits have been attracting life to the area for thousands of years; more recently, during the late 1800s, St Agnes was the hub of tin and copper mining, but discoveries of Mesolithic remains dating to 10,000 BC have been found, as well as evidence of habitation from the Bronze Age, when the tin and copper would have been used for making tools and weapons.

location: Trevone Bay, Padstow, Cornwall, TR8 4BU
notes: Trevone Bay is a gently shelving, sandy beach surrounded by high cliffs, featuring the iconic Trevone Round Hole and the popular tidal pool. Trevone Bay was the winner of a Blue Flag Award and Seaside Award in 2024, which celebrates the commitment to environment, water quality, and safety of the beach. Near the bustling harbour town of Padstow in North Cornwall, Trevone Bay is a hive of activity, on and offshore. With the South West Coast Path passing over the clifftops, walkers can delight in the spectacular coastal scenery and views to Hawkers Cove, the Camel Estuary and beyond, and pass the fascinating 80 ft blow-hole known as ‘Round Hole’, that was formed by a collapsed sea cave, and is just one of the reasons the area is of great geological significance having been designated as a Site of Special Scientific Interest (SSSI). For those keen to discover the marine wildlife, find Rocky beach around the small headland, aptly named for its rocky outcrop, perfect for rock-pooling. There’s also the Trevone tidal pool, one of the largest on the Cornish coast, it’s affectionately known by locals as ‘Tinker Bunny’s Bathing Pool.’ Trevone Bay is lifeguarded between 10am - 6pm daily between 18th May and 29th September (2024). Dogs are banned from the beach between May 15th and September 30th, between the hours of 10am and 6pm. Dogs are welcome at all other times.

location: Towan Beach, Newquay, Cornwall, TR7 1EA
notes: Towan Beach is at the heart of Newquay, one of the liveliest and most visited towns in Cornwall. Situated at the bottom of a steeply sloping hill, the beach is bordered to the west by the harbour and at the east by 'The Island' a towering rocky outcrop which is connected to the mainland by a suspension footbridge. 'The Island,' which is now a luxurious holiday rental, was the unique home of the inventor of the spark plug, Alexander Lodge, who built it in 1901, and is believed to have hosted esteemed guests such as Sir Arthur Conan Doyle.

location: Swanpool Beach, Swanpool, Falmouth, Cornwall, TR11 5BG
notes: Dogs are not allowed on the beach between 1 July - 31 August, 10am to 6pm (2023)

location: Watergate Bay, Cornwall, TR8 4AA
notes: Watergate Bay beach is around 3 miles from Newquay on the North Cornwall coast, stretching out for two miles of golden sand, imposing cliffs, and untamed sea. Spectators, surfers, and world-class kite surfers flock here for the enormous waves providing a spectacular sight on any day. Privately owned, the beach is dog-friendly year-round and if the sea-breeze gets too fresh, there are cafes and restaurants close by to shelter and warm up in.

location: Carlyon Bay, Cornwall
notes: Carlyon Bay Beach transforms into a vibrant event destination each summer, blending seaside charm with dynamic entertainment. From May to September, Shoreside hosts live music every Friday night, featuring local rock bands, silent discos, karaoke, and quiz nights—all free to attend. The beach also offers yoga sessions, open-air theatre, and unique events like beach Frisbee golf and the National Beach Cricket Competition. With pop-up food stalls and a lively atmosphere, Carlyon Bay Beach is a must-visit for both locals and tourists seeking summer fun.

location: Towan Beach - The Roseland, Bohortha, The Roseland, Cornwall, TR2 5LW
notes: Towan Beach on The Roseland Peninsula is a quiet, south-east facing sand and shingle bay near St Mawes and is just one of the many serene, secluded beaches along the beautiful unspoilt headland. Within an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty, this haven at the tip of St Gerrans Bay is dog-friendly year-round, its vast shoreline backed by low grass-covered cliff never getting too crowded, even at the height of summer. Many people visit Towan via the South West Coast Path whilst on the way to the historic St Anthony’s Head Lighthouse at the end of the peninsula. The lighthouse was built by Trinity House in 1835 to guide vessels safely into Falmouth Harbour past the treacherous Manacles reef, but famously was also featured in the children’s TV series Fraggle Rock.

location: Summerleaze Beach, Bude, Cornwall, EX23 8HN
notes: Summerleaze Beach is an RNLI lifeguarded beach, patrolled from the 4th of May to the 29th of September between 10am and 6pm. The beach is additionally patrolled in the Easter school holidays and October half-term. As well as weekends between 20th April - 28th April and 5th October and 20th October. (2024) Dogs must be on leads from 21st May to 30th September from 10am-6pm. There is disabled access from the carpark, disabled toilets and a disabled sand chair is also available from the Summerleaze Beach Office 01288 352226. Surfing Info: Good when everywhere else is maxed out. Right handers at mid tide also lefts at low tide. Suitable for: Beginners through to experienced surfers. Dangers: North of beach rocky, also sea pool hidden at high tide, with rocks in the pool. Strong rip (river) and also crowded in the busy season. Lots of bouncing, cross waves. Tides: Surfable at all tides. Wind: E/SE offshore. AdSurf is a charity that was set up in 2022, with the aim of including everyone who wants to experience the benefits of the sea and surfing, by providing accessible and adaptive surfing to people with disabilities, mental health conditions and neurodiversity.

location: Talland Bay Beach, Polperro, Cornwall, PL13 2JA
notes: Talland Bay Beach is nestled midway between Looe and Polperro; its picturesque two coves are separated by a rocky outcrop at high tide and flanked by rolling hills. Within an Area of Outstanding Beauty, Talland Bay is unspoilt and serene; Talland Sands is the bigger of the two coves, with sand at both high tide and low tide, whilst to the east, Rotterdam Beach is small and less sandy. Both coves boast beautiful crystal-clear sea and are suitable for swimming. With the tide out there are plenty of rock pools to discover between the beaches, great fishing spots, and for those who like to explore further, the boiler of the French trawler ‘Marguerite’ lies amongst the rocks, where it ran aground in 1922. There are cafes at both beaches and seasonal toilets near the main beach. Please Note: Access by road to Talland is along narrow lanes and steep hills and parking is limited.
